strengths: The intervention is simple, differentiable, and requires no auxiliary objectives. Applying SEM to actor representations could be practically useful if its benefits hold under controlled comparisons.

The empirical study is broad, spanning FastTD3, FastSAC, SimBaV2 variants, PPO, and FQL across continuous control, Atari, multitask learning, and offline-to-online adaptation. Many per-task curves show substantial improvements in early learning.

Actor-only, critic-only, and joint interventions, representation diagnostics, and extensive FastTD3 hyperparameter ablations provide useful exploratory evidence. Six seeds for continuous-control experiments and per-task appendix results are positive features.
weaknesses: The principal comparison is confounded by architectural changes. Appendix E describes replacing Linear→ReLU→Linear with SEM→Linear, apparently removing a learned layer as well as changing the activation. Without depth- and parameter-controlled baselines, the gains and runtime results cannot be attributed specifically to simplex geometry. Varying L and V also changes representation capacity without adequate matched controls.

Theorem 1 is not established. Appendix B asserts, rather than proves, that drift systematically reduces covariance rank and activation probabilities; these consequences do not follow from non-stationarity alone. Equation 7 is false as stated: constant nonzero features have zero centered covariance but can yield nonzero head gradients. Equation 8 also factors activation probability from gradient magnitude without the necessary assumptions. These are substantive problems in the claimed formal explanation.

The central claim that SEM prevents representation collapse is mathematically unsupported. Unit mass bounds feature norms but does not bound centered covariance away from zero: every input can map to the same simplex point. Softmax also permits saturated, nearly vanishing gradients. Consequently, the claims of preserved diversity and sustained gradient energy require additional assumptions or substantially narrower wording.

Novelty is limited to deploying and studying an existing representation layer in additional actor–critic settings; the paper acknowledges prior SEM use in TD-MPC2. Although the experimental breadth is valuable, comparisons do not sufficiently isolate SEM from simpler normalization, bounded-activation, or reduced-capacity alternatives. Gumbel-ST, vector quantization, and CReLU comparisons lack enough implementation and tuning detail to establish a convincing advantage.

Important evaluation details are missing or inconsistent. Default SEM temperatures and complete L/V configurations are not specified across methods; aggregate normalization and uncertainty-band definitions are unclear. Humanoid plots labeled 'Environment Steps' do not explain whether counts represent individual transitions or parallel simulator steps, which particularly matters when varying environment count. The main text describes Atari-10, while Appendix D and Figure 19 describe or show 27 games.

Several mechanistic and efficiency conclusions exceed the evidence. Figure 6 shows SEM entropy and action standard deviation generally increasing during learning, contrary to the accompanying description of decreasing trends. Reduced critic disagreement does not establish value calibration, and diagnostics on changing policy distributions do not establish causality. Table 2 covers only five tasks, lacks hardware and timing uncertainty, and includes slowdowns, so it supports roughly comparable runtime rather than an unconditional claim of no speed loss.

strengths: The proposed intervention is simple and practically attractive: group-wise softmax representations require no auxiliary objective and can be incorporated into existing actor–critic agents.

The empirical study is broad, covering FastTD3, FastTD3–SimBaV2, FastSAC, PPO, and exploratory offline-to-online experiments. The reported learning curves show meaningful improvements across several settings, with six seeds for continuous-control experiments.

Useful ablations investigate actor versus critic placement, representation dimensions, alternative discrete representations, and robustness to several FastTD3 design choices. The strong results from actor-only intervention are an interesting empirical finding.
weaknesses: The formal analysis in Appendix B is not a valid proof of Theorem 1. Non-stationarity is asserted to cause covariance deflation and reduced ReLU activation probabilities without assumptions or derivations establishing either implication. Equation (7) is false in general: constant nonzero features have zero covariance but can produce nonzero gradients for the linear head. Equation (8) also factors dependent quantities without justification. These problems undermine the claimed theoretical explanation.

The central collapse-prevention argument confuses nonzero feature norms with nonzero covariance. Identical simplex embeddings for every input satisfy the unit-mass constraint while having zero covariance and no representational diversity. Consequently, SEM does not by itself guarantee the claimed covariance preservation, effective rank, or sustained gradient energy. The paper repeatedly presents these properties more strongly than its evidence supports.

The architecture comparison is insufficiently controlled. Appendix E describes replacing Linear–ReLU–Linear with SEM–Linear, suggesting that depth and parameter count change alongside the representation constraint. Without matched-depth and matched-capacity controls, gains cannot be cleanly attributed to simplex geometry. The L/V ablations also change representation capacity. Direct comparisons against simple bounded activations, LayerNorm, and L2 feature normalization would help isolate the mechanism; the SimBaV2 experiment does not replace these controls.

Novelty is primarily empirical: SEM is an existing method, and the paper acknowledges its prior use in TD-MPC2. Applying it to model-free actors could be valuable, but the incremental methodological contribution requires especially convincing attribution and analysis. Current diagnostics establish correlations rather than causation, and lower TD error or agreement between critics does not establish value calibration against actual returns.

Important evaluation and reproduction details are missing or ambiguous. The hyperparameter tables omit the actual SEM temperature and complete per-setting L/V configurations. Return normalization and uncertainty bands are insufficiently specified. In the parallel-environment ablations, it is unclear whether the horizontal axis counts vectorized simulator steps or total transitions; this distinction is essential when claiming sample-efficiency improvements across different environment counts.

There are substantive inconsistencies in experimental reporting. Figures 20 and 21 display the same G1 learning curves, although Figure 20 is captioned as 16 H1 tasks. The main text instead describes 12 H1 and 12 G1 tasks. Atari is repeatedly called Atari-10 although Appendix D reports 27 games, and Figure 19 labels its PPO baseline as FastTD3. These discrepancies make the precise scope and provenance of the results difficult to verify.

The runtime and transfer claims need tighter qualification. Table 2 reports timings for only five tasks, without hardware or timing variability, and includes slowdowns such as 2:31 to 2:42 on walking; this supports roughly comparable runtime rather than an unconditional absence of overhead. The Booster T1 experiment is simulation-only according to Appendix D, so it does not demonstrate real-robot transfer of SEM.

strengths: SEM is a simple, differentiable architectural intervention without auxiliary losses. Applying it to actor representations is a practically useful direction.

The experimental coverage is substantial: multiple actor–critic algorithms, humanoid control, pixel-based PPO, multitask learning, and offline-to-online learning. Many learning curves show meaningful improvements in early performance.

The paper includes useful actor-versus-critic placement ablations, comparisons with alternative representations, and sensitivity studies across several FastTD3 design choices. Six seeds for continuous-control experiments and per-task curves strengthen the empirical evidence.

Equation (7) incorrectly bounds gradient energy using centered covariance: constant nonzero features can have zero covariance but nonzero weight gradients. Equation (8) also requires assumptions to separate activation probability from gradient magnitude. These issues undermine the claimed theoretical explanation.

The claim that simplex constraints prevent representation collapse is false in general. Every input can map to the same simplex vector, giving zero covariance despite nonzero feature norm. Unit mass guarantees neither feature diversity nor preserved gradient energy. The paper repeatedly conflates bounded feature magnitude with protection against collapse.

The architecture comparison has an important confound. Appendix E describes replacing Linear–ReLU–Linear with SEM–Linear, changing network depth and potentially parameter count alongside representation geometry. Matched-depth and matched-capacity controls are needed to attribute improvements specifically to SEM. Direct comparisons against simpler bounded or normalized features are also missing.

Evaluation and reproducibility details are incomplete. The main experiments do not clearly specify SEM's L, V, and temperature settings; normalized-return calculations and uncertainty bands are insufficiently defined. The meaning of environment steps under parallel simulation also needs clarification, particularly when comparing different environment counts. Atari is described as Atari-10, while Appendix D and Figure 19 report 27 games, and that figure labels the baseline FastTD3 despite the stated PPO setup.

The mechanistic evidence is correlational and narrower than the conclusions. Diagnostics concentrate on two humanoid tasks with separately evolving data distributions. Smaller TD errors or disagreement between critics do not establish calibrated value estimates, and higher feature rank alone does not demonstrate that preventing collapse causes the performance gains.

The transformation is established prior work and has already appeared in RL through TD-MPC2, so the contribution primarily rests on convincing empirical isolation and analysis. The broad positive results are promising, but the architectural confound and unsound theoretical claims leave that contribution insufficiently established for acceptance. Runtime measurements on five tasks, without variability or clear hardware details, also support only approximate cost parity rather than the categorical claim of no runtime loss.

Equation (6) incorrectly bounds gradient energy using centered covariance: constant nonzero features can have zero covariance but nonzero head gradients. Equation (7) also requires dependence assumptions that are not supplied. These problems undermine the claimed theoretical explanation.

The central claim that simplex constraints prevent representation collapse is false in general. Every input can map to the same simplex vector, yielding zero centered covariance despite unit mass in each block. Thus the argument in Section 3 that normalization keeps tr(Σ) bounded away from zero confuses second moments with covariance. Softmax can also saturate, so sustained gradient energy does not follow from bounded representations.

The experimental comparisons do not adequately isolate the proposed mechanism. Figure 2 includes LayerNorm within the SEM module, while Appendix E describes replacing a Linear–ReLU sequence with SEM. The exact projections, widths, and parameter counts are insufficiently specified. Architecture-matched controls, especially LayerNorm without group-wise softmax and matched bottleneck widths, are needed to attribute improvements specifically to simplex geometry.

Establishing its usefulness in model-free actors could be valuable, but the contribution depends heavily on convincing causal analysis and controlled comparisons, which remain incomplete.

The diagnostics support correlations rather than the stronger mechanistic claims. Reduced disagreement between two critics does not establish calibration against actual returns. The absolute-activation dormancy metric is also difficult to compare across ReLU and strictly positive softmax features. Higher feature rank and lower TD errors do not by themselves establish that preventing collapse causes the performance improvements.

The manuscript does not clearly specify temperature and final L/V settings across algorithms, continuous-control return normalization, or whether plotted environment steps count individual transitions or vectorized simulator steps. The last distinction is essential when comparing different numbers of parallel environments. Runtime results lack hardware details and uncertainty, and include slowdowns on some tasks, making the categorical claim of no runtime loss too strong.

The empirical scope is substantial, covering FastTD3, FastSAC, PPO, SimBaV2, and offline-to-online FQL across continuous-control and pixel-based tasks. Several aggregate curves show meaningful improvements.

The paper includes extensive ablations on placement, simplex dimensions, parallelism, replay settings, and competing regularizers, generally using six seeds for continuous control. Reporting the mixed PQN results is also valuable.

Equation (6) is false for constant nonzero features: their covariance is zero, but the linear-head gradient can be nonzero. Equation (7) also factorizes dependent quantities without justification.

The claimed protection against representation collapse confuses feature magnitude with diversity. Unit simplex mass does not keep covariance trace positive: an encoder producing the same probability vector for every input has zero covariance. Softmax can also saturate and suppress gradients. Consequently, the claims that SEM prevents covariance deflation and sustains gradient energy are unsupported.

The architectural comparisons do not cleanly isolate the proposed mechanism. Figure 2 includes LayerNorm inside SEM, while Appendix E describes replacing a Linear–ReLU block with SEM. Varying L and V also changes representation width. Matched architecture and width controls, including LayerNorm alone, are needed to distinguish simplex geometry from normalization and bottleneck effects; the L2 feature-normalization baseline does not resolve this.

HumanoidBench plots label their axes as environment steps while using 128 parallel environments, without specifying whether counts represent total transitions or vectorized steps. This is especially consequential when comparing different environment counts. The normalization used for aggregate continuous-control returns is also insufficiently specified.

The diagnostics establish correlations rather than the claimed mechanism. Lower TD errors and agreement between critics do not establish value calibration; both critics can agree while being wrong. Most detailed diagnostics concern two tasks, and the strongest gains occur with actor-only SEM, leaving the proposed critic-collapse explanation insufficiently tested.

The algorithmic novelty is limited because SEM is an existing transformation already used in TD-MPC2, as Appendix A acknowledges. Its application to model-free actors could still be a useful contribution, but that makes reliable attribution and evaluation particularly important.

Reproducibility and efficiency claims need stronger support. The hyperparameter tables omit SEM temperature and comprehensive per-setting SEM configurations. Table 2 reports only five tasks, without hardware specifications or timing variability, and includes slowdowns such as 2:31 versus 2:42 on walking. These measurements suggest broadly comparable runtime, not the categorical claim of no runtime loss.

strengths: The proposed intervention is simple and practically appealing: applying grouped softmax embeddings to actor networks requires no auxiliary learning objective and appears inexpensive.

The empirical evaluation is broad, covering FastTD3, FastTD3–SimBaV2, FastSAC, and PPO across continuous control and Atari, with additional multitask and offline-to-online experiments. Reported improvements across these settings provide meaningful evidence of practical utility.

The paper includes extensive ablations of intervention location, simplex dimensions, parallelism, replay capacity, batch size, and algorithmic components. Appendix H also compares against numerous representation and plasticity interventions.
Six-seed continuous-control experiments, per-task learning curves, confidence intervals, and disclosure of inconsistent PQN results are valuable aspects of the evaluation.
weaknesses: The formal analysis is technically unsound. Appendix B asserts that non-stationarity necessarily causes covariance deflation and reduced activation probabilities without establishing either implication. Equation (6) is false in general: constant nonzero features have zero covariance but can produce nonzero gradients of the linear head. Equation (7) also factors dependent quantities without justification. These are substantive problems with the claimed theorem, not merely missing exposition.

The central claim that simplex constraints prevent representation collapse is unsupported. Identical simplex embeddings for every input satisfy all normalization constraints while having zero covariance and no representational diversity. Unit mass bounds feature norms away from zero but does not bound covariance trace away from zero, contrary to Section 3. The empirical findings should be distinguished from a general collapse-prevention guarantee.

The experiments do not adequately isolate the source of improvement. Figure 2 includes LayerNorm inside the SEM module, while Appendix E describes replacing a Linear–ReLU block, and the L/V sweeps change representation dimensionality. A matched architecture and width control with LayerNorm alone is needed to distinguish simplex geometry from normalization, bottleneck size, and parameter-count effects. The existing feature-normalization comparisons do not resolve all these confounds.

The mechanistic diagnostics are primarily correlational and collected under different learned policies and data distributions. Reduced critic disagreement or TD error does not establish better calibration against actual returns, and higher feature rank does not demonstrate that collapse prevention caused the performance gain. The strongest improvements from actor-only interventions make the asserted critic-stabilization mechanism especially important to test directly.

Important evaluation and reproduction details remain unclear: the default SEM temperature, complete per-setting SEM configurations, continuous-control return normalization, and whether plotted environment steps count vectorized steps or total transitions. The latter matters particularly when comparing different numbers of parallel environments. Table 2 provides only five timing comparisons without hardware details or uncertainty, and includes slowdowns, so it does not establish the blanket claim of no runtime loss.

There are material reporting inconsistencies. Figures 31 and 32 repeat the same 20 G1 task plots, although Figure 31 claims to show 16 H1 tasks; Section 5 instead mentions 12 H1 and 12 G1 tasks. Figure 28's caption identifies FastSAC while its legend identifies FastTD3–SimBaV2. These discrepancies obscure which experiments support the claimed breadth.

The methodological novelty is limited because SEM is an existing technique already used in RL, as the paper acknowledges for TD-MPC2. Establishing its value specifically in model-free actors could be a worthwhile contribution, but the unresolved technical errors and experimental attribution issues prevent the current evidence from meeting the acceptance threshold.
